Description: An archive of 35 legal papyri, dated AD 94-134, found in March 1961 by a team led by Yigael Yadin in a concealed hiding place in the Cave of Letters at Nahal Hever on the western shore of the Dead Sea. The papers were hidden in a leather satchel by Babatha, daughter of Shim'on, a Jewish woman of Maoza in Roman Arabia, who had fled to the cave with other Jewish refugees at the end of the Bar Kokhba revolt in AD 135. The archive contains marriage contracts, deeds of gift, court documents and records of date-palm orchards, including an orchard her father bought at Maoza in AD 99 and later gave to her.
Interpretations: Babatha's papers are the fullest surviving picture of an ordinary Jewish woman's legal life under Rome: she owned orchards, married twice, went to court, and kept every deed. The archive shows Jewish, Nabatean and Roman law operating side by side in one woman's affairs, and it gives the Bar Kokhba revolt a human scale, since these are the papers of people who hid and died rather than surrender them.
BiblicalSignificance: The archive illuminates daily Jewish life in Roman Arabia a generation after the New Testament, when the early church was spreading through exactly this world of deeds, courts and orchards.
DiscoveryLocation: Cave of Letters, Nahal Hever, Judean Desert
